perfil_profesional: La Dra. Gómez es profesora titular en la Escuela de Medicina y Ciencias de la Salud de la Universidad del Rosario en Colombia y lidera el grupo de Estudios en Microbiología Traslacional y Enfermedades Emergentes MICROS. Es Bacterióloga y Laboratorista Clínica del Colegio Mayor de Antioquia en Colombia. Comenzó su entrenamiento y carrera como investigadora en el área de la Micología Médica con el grupo de la Dra. Ángela Restrepo en Medellín Colombia en 1990. Obtuvo su Doctorado (PhD) en Micología Médica en el King´s College London, Universidad de Londres, Reino Unido y luego un Posdoctorado con la misma universidad (proyecto financiado por la Wellcome Trust para científicos de países tropicales y en desarrollo) y segundo Posdoctorado con el University College London que incluyo trabajo cooperativo con el Aberdeen Fungal Group en Escocia. Trabajó como jefe de la Unidad de Desarrollo Diagnóstico en Micología en el Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Atlanta, USA. Su interés en investigación ha estado enfocado en el área de diagnóstico y caracterización de hongos patógenos especialmente en histoplasmosis, paracoccidioidomycosis y otras micosis causadas por hongos oportunistas. Ha liderado y participado en varios estudios multicéntricos que han contribuido al desarrollo y validación de métodos inmunológicos y moleculares especialmente en pacientes inmunocomprometidos. La Dra. Gómez ha trabajado activamente con colegas en las Américas para crear y coordinar actividades del “Histoplasmosis Advocacy Group” (iHAG) que se ha enfocado en mejorar el diagnóstico, tratamiento y establecer el impacto de esta micosis en la salud pública. Es miembro del Council y Vice presidenta desde el 2018 del “International Society for Human and Animal Mycology” (ISHAM) que ha enfocado sus esfuerzos en programas educativos, en reforzar la colaboración internacional a través de grupos trabajo y en abogar para incluir las micosis en las agendas de salud pública. Ha publicado numerosos artículos, capítulos de libros, coeditado un libro y regularmente enseña y organiza cursos en el área de micología médica para estudiantes de pre grado y posgrado.

Tipo de proyecto: Investigación y desarrollo Technology transfer and evaluation of a novel antigen detection test in urine for improving and expanding the capacity to diagnose histoplasmosis in Colombia and Latin America. Inicio: Mayo 2008 Fin: Diciembre 2013 Duración 72 Resumen Abstract Introduction: Histoplasmosis is the most frequent endemic mycosis in Colombia and in the Americas and is an important cause of mortality in patients with HIV infection, especially in countries with limited access to antiretroviral therapies and diagnostic tests. Objectives: 1. Transfer and validate in Colombia an ELISA antigen capture assay that detects a polysaccharide antigen of H. capsulatum. 2. Validate the technique in a cohort of Colombian patients. 3. Build capacity to promptly diagnose histoplasmosis in Colombia, and in the near future also in other Latin American countries. Materials and methods: A prospective cohort of HIV infected patients from La María Hospital (May 2008 to August 2011) was designed. A case of suspected histoplasmosis was defined as a person presenting with at least three of the following five criteria: fever, pancytopenia, weight loss, radiological evidence of pulmonary involvement or skin/mucosal lesions. A confirmed case of histoplasmosis was defined as a person with a positive culture. A total of 175 urine samples were collected: 76 from patients from La María Hospital, 44 from healthy individuals and 55 from patients with other infectious diseases. Results: The sensitivity of the H. capsulatum ELISA was 85% in proven cases and overall specificity was 98% when including urine controls from patients with other diseases and healthy individuals. Conclusions: The transferred and validated assay was reproducible and the results in Colombia compare well with those obtained by the CDC in Atlanta. In an endemic country such as Colombia, access to a rapid, sensitive and specific test could impact patient outcomes by decreasing time to diagnosis, allowing early treatment of PDH and reducing the mortality caused by this disease.

Tipo de proyecto: Investigación y desarrollo Development of novel molecular methods for the diagnosis of histoplasmosis Inicio: Noviembre 2013 Fin: Diciembre 2016 Duración Resumen Histoplasmosis is one of the most frequent fungal infections (mycoses) afflicting persons with HIV/AIDS. Histoplasmosis causes significant morbidity and mortality in human immunodeficiency virus-infected individuals, particularly in those countries with limited access to rapid diagnostics or antiretroviral therapies, with up to 48% mortality reported. Despite the absence of official figures for Colombia, as this mycosis is not a reportable disease, a national study conducted by the CIB and the Colombian National Institute of Health (INS) revealed that among 434 histoplasmosis cases reported, 70% corresponded to AIDS patients. A parallel clinical study by the CIB showed that 30% of these patients died in the first three weeks post diagnosis. Histoplasmosis is under-diagnosed in Colombia and other countries in the Americas where the disease is highly endemic. The diagnosis in Colombia typically relies on conventional blood cultures, which are positive in only approximately 50% of cases and may take up to 6 weeks. Immunological tests that detect antibodies are not very sensitive (38.8%-70%) and may often be negative in immunodeficient patients. A few molecular approaches have been developed, but DNA-based diagnosis has not yet been established as a regular diagnostic tool for histoplasmosis and no PCR assay is commercially available. There is a need to develop and extensively validate new methods such as real time PCR assays targeting genes that are highly specific for Histoplasma species. Objetives: The primary objective of this international collaboration is to develop and validate new molecular methods for the rapid diagnosis of histoplasmosis and for the follow up of patients during therapy. An animal model and a clinical study (cohort of AIDS patients) will be developed to determine and statistically analyze sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values of the new molecular tests (real time PCR). The application of the new methodologies to promptly diagnose this disorder should decrease mortality in this susceptible group of patients.
